headline: Certification has become the ground Gulf suppliers compete on
deck: When every supplier claims performance, the ones who can document it under a recognised standard have removed the argument.
excerpt: Across three exhibitions in two weeks, Gulf buyers asked the same questions: certification, tested performance, warranties, lifecycle cost, spare parts, real project references. Each is a way of converting a claim into something checkable.
content:
Three exhibitions in two weeks — construction in Riyadh, industry alongside it, power in Dubai — produced a consistent pattern in what buyers were asking, and it was not about price.

The questions were about certification, tested performance, lifecycle cost, warranties, local after-sales support, spare parts availability and real project references. Every one of those converts a claim into something a buyer can check before committing.

That shift is what a market looks like when supply catches up with demand. Where capacity is short, a buyer takes what is available. Where there are alternatives, the buyer can insist on evidence, and suppliers who cannot produce it lose on ground that has nothing to do with the quality of their product.

Certification is the most structured form of that evidence and the most misunderstood. A certificate is not a statement that a product is good. It is a statement that a specified property was measured by a competent party under a defined method, and its usefulness depends entirely on whether the method reflects the conditions of use.

That last point is where the Gulf differs. A product certified for performance at European ambient temperatures may behave differently at Saudi design conditions, and a buyer who accepts the certificate without checking the test basis has bought a number rather than a performance. Eurovent's desert certification argument, made to Saudi HVAC buyers at Big 5, is precisely about that gap.

Embodied carbon documentation is the newest addition to the list and it follows the same logic. Where an environmental product declaration is uneconomic to produce, a structured estimate under a recognised methodology fills the blank. Albion's use of the CIBSE TM65 method across its cast-iron valve range, shown by Galaxy Engineering on the Big 5 Impact Trail, is an example of a category producing a defensible figure where previously it produced none.

For the supplier the strategic consequence is clear enough. In a market where volume runs through a narrow band of specifications — reinforced concrete at 30 to 60 MPa, structural steel in S275 and S355 — nobody differentiates on specification. Differentiation comes from consistency, documentation, and the ability to prove a claim under a method the buyer recognises.

For the buyer it is a governance question. Asking for certification is easy; reading it, understanding the test basis and enforcing it through procurement is a technical capability that large clients have and smaller ones frequently do not. That asymmetry is one of the real differences between the concentrated and fragmented halves of the Saudi construction market.
author: BrentDesk Staff
